title: Understanding the Mpemba Effect through a Rule of Thumb
abstract: In the Mpemba effect, a system prepared farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than one prepared closer to it. Its persistence across diverse systems, and under different dynamics of the same system, suggests that it is largely rooted in equilibrium properties, with the dynamics deciding only which mode relaxes slowest. Here we propose a simple rule of thumb for anticipating the Mpemba effect: the effect is expected when a single low-order equilibrium moment is nonmonotonic in temperature. The bath singles out this moment as the slowest to relax, so that its displacement from its bath value sets the amplitude of the slowest relaxation mode. We establish this relation exactly for low-dimensional Ornstein--Uhlenbeck processes. We then extend the rule to mean-field models by approximating their relaxation near the final equilibrium state by an Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process. For the mean-field Ising antiferromagnet, which we solve exactly in the thermodynamic limit, this approximation reproduces the main structure of the Mpemba phase diagram, including strong effects far from any phase transition. Finally, we give a general prescription for mean-field systems: identify the slowest symmetry-allowed moment of the normal coordinates at the bath, and follow its equilibrium value as a function of preparation temperature. This offers a practical route from equilibrium observables to anomalous relaxation without diagonalizing the dynamics.
summary: This paper proposes a general rule of thumb to predict the Mpemba effect—the faster relaxation from a highly non-equilibrium state. It achieves this by showing that the effect is linked to the nonmonotonic temperature dependence of a single, slow-relaxing equilibrium moment. The methodology is general, applying to mean-field models by analyzing the slow symmetry-allowed moment.
main_problem: The paper aims to provide a general, equilibrium-based rule of thumb to predict the Mpemba effect—where a system prepared far from equilibrium relaxes faster than one prepared close to it.
main_result: The Mpemba effect is predicted when a single low-order equilibrium moment of the system's order parameters exhibits nonmonotonic behavior as a function of the preparation temperature.
method: The analysis involves linearizing the master equation near the bath equilibrium and analyzing the slow relaxation modes (eigenfunctions and coefficients) derived from the Fokker-Planck operator.
model_or_system: The study analyzes general overdamped systems, specifically deriving results for the 1D Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process and extending the framework to mean-field models like the Ising antiferromagnet.
key_observables: The slow mode coefficient ($a_1$), the Kullback-Leibler (KL) Divergence ($D_{KL}$), and the temperature dependence of equilibrium moments (e.g., $\langle x angle_T$).
important_parameters: Preparation temperature ($T$), bath temperature ($T_b$), and the nonmonotonicity of equilibrium moments.
main_assumptions: The analysis often relies on approximating the dynamics near equilibrium using an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process, and the mean-field model uses a leading-order approximation in $1/N$.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the mechanism of the quench, showing how the slow mode coefficient ($a_1$) exhibits nonmonotonicity, and compare exact dynamics against harmonic approximations for mean-field systems.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing simple 1D systems (OU process) to 2D uncoupled coordinates, culminating in the application to the mean-field Ising antiferromagnet to establish a general, practical prescription.
why_interesting: The connection drawn between non-equilibrium relaxation anomalies (Mpemba effect) and purely equilibrium properties (nonmonotonicity of moments) provides a powerful, predictive tool for understanding complex dynamics in statistical physics.
